reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Lumbar spinal stenosis classically causes neurogenic claudication, with leg pain, heaviness, or numbness on standing and walking that eases with sitting or leaning forward
The forward-flexed posture that relieves symptoms explains why patients often report easier walking uphill or when leaning on a trolley
Cervical stenosis can produce cervical myelopathy, with clumsy hands, gait imbalance, and upper motor neuron signs in the legs
It is usually a degenerative condition of older adults driven by disc bulging, facet hypertrophy, and ligamentum flavum thickening narrowing the canal or neural foramina
Distinguishing neurogenic from vascular claudication rests on the posture-dependent pattern, preserved peripheral pulses, and provocation by standing rather than a fixed walking distance
Initial management is usually conservative with physiotherapy, activity modification, and analgesia; decompressive surgery is considered for disabling or progressive symptoms
Progressive myelopathy in cervical stenosis or any sphincter disturbance warrants prompt specialist assessment
Imaging findings of stenosis are common with age and must be correlated with symptoms rather than treated in isolation
reference.pathophysiology: Spinal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina that compresses the cord, cauda equina, or nerve roots. It is most often degenerative, resulting from intervertebral disc bulging, osteophyte formation, facet joint hypertrophy, and buckling or thickening of the ligamentum flavum, sometimes compounded by spondylolisthesis or congenitally narrow canals. In the lumbar spine, compression of the cauda equina and roots produces neurogenic claudication, aggravated by extension which further narrows the canal and relieved by flexion. In the cervical spine, cord compression can cause myelopathy through direct pressure and ischaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of myelopathy in cervical disease (e.g. tumour, demyelination)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the relevant spinal region to characterise the level and severity of compression
CT or CT myelography when MRI is contraindicated or bony detail is needed
Plain radiographs including flexion-extension views to assess instability or spondylolisthesis
Nerve conduction studies or EMG when peripheral neuropathy is a competing diagnosis
Ankle-brachial index or vascular studies to exclude arterial claudication
redFlags: New or progressive cauda equina symptoms such as saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, or bowel dysfunction requiring urgent evaluation
Rapidly progressive cervical myelopathy with worsening gait or hand function
Bilateral neurological deficit or significant motor weakness
Features suggesting infection or malignancy, such as fever, night pain, or weight loss
reference.prognosis: Symptoms often follow a fluctuating or slowly progressive course; many patients are managed conservatively for years, and decompression can relieve claudication and stabilise myelopathy, though established cord damage in cervical disease may not fully reverse.
pitfalls: Treating incidental imaging stenosis that does not match the clinical picture
Confusing neurogenic with vascular claudication and missing peripheral arterial disease
Overlooking early cervical myelopathy, mistaking gait and hand changes for ageing
Failing to recognise cauda equina features as an emergency
management: Begin conservative management with physiotherapy, activity modification, flexion-based exercise and simple analgesia
Add neuropathic-pain agents such as gabapentinoids and consider epidural corticosteroid injection for radicular symptoms
Offer decompressive surgery, such as laminectomy with fusion where instability or spondylolisthesis coexists, for disabling or progressive neurogenic claudication
Treat cervical myelopathy with timely surgical decompression to arrest progression, as established cord damage may not reverse
Distinguish neurogenic from vascular claudication before treatment using the posture-dependent pattern, peripheral pulses and ankle-brachial index
Monitor for progressive deficit and escalate urgently if myelopathy, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or cauda equina features emerge
